props.title: The Last Tycoon

sections.content: Elia Kazan's The Last Tycoon represents Hollywood's fascinating attempt to adapt F. Scott Fitzgerald's unfinished novel about the movie industry's golden age. With Robert De Niro delivering a mesmerizing performance as Monroe Stahr (based on real-life producer Irving Thalberg), the film captures the intricate power dynamics of 1930s Hollywood. Like Sunset Boulevard (1950) and The Bad and the Beautiful (1952), it peels back the glamorous facade to reveal the machinery of classic moviemaking. Harold Pinter's screenplay maintains the novel's elegiac tone while crystallizing the tragic arc of a brilliant producer consumed by his own perfectionism.

sections.content: The film's production context is equally compelling, arriving during a transformative period in American cinema. Released between The Godfather Part II (1974) and New York, New York (1977), De Niro's portrayal of Stahr showcases the emerging naturalistic acting style that would define the era. Director Elia Kazan, making what would be his final film, brings his characteristic psychological complexity to the material, though the result is more subdued than his earlier classics like On the Waterfront (1954). SUBHEAD: Hollywood Self-Reflection

The Last Tycoon joins a rich tradition of Hollywood examining itself, though its approach is more elegiac than satirical predecessors like Singin' in the Rain (1952). The film's detailed recreation of 1930s studio operations, from soundstage politics to executive boardroom tensions, provides a valuable historical document of the studio system. This attention to period detail would influence later Hollywood-on-Hollywood films like The Aviator (2004) and Mank (2020).
